citation.title: On the reliability of published findings using the regression discontinuity design in political science

standing_assumptions:
The article (Research and Politics, April–June 2023, pp. 1–12; printed page numbers equal PDF page numbers) is a survey and reanalysis of 45 published regression discontinuity (RD) studies. It states no theorem, proposition, lemma or proof and displays no formula; its mathematical content is in running text, in Tables 1–3 and in Figures 1–5. Every passage of the article quoted in this file was read from the page images. The official online supplement (Sections S1–S9, 23 pp.) is staged only as a text extraction, with no rendered pages; the few supplement passages quoted here (Section S4, Section S9, Figure S9) are transcribed from that extraction and are marked as such wherever they occur.
(S1) Estimand and identification. p. 3 (PDF p. 3), section ‘Why is it hard to estimate RD effects?’: “The causal effect studied in the RD design is the difference between the expected treated and control potential outcomes at a cutoff where treatment assignment changes in a discontinuous fashion. If the conditional expectation function of the outcome were known, this effect can be calculated without error under an assumption that the conditional expectation functions of the potential outcomes are continuous at the cut point. In other words, the RD effect is identified under a continuity assumption.” The paper uses no symbols for these objects. The targets write $X$ for the running variable, $c$ for the cutoff, $Y(1)$ and $Y(0)$ for the potential outcomes, $D = \mathbf{1}\{X \ge c\}$ for treatment in a sharp design, and $\tau = E[Y(1)\mid X = c] - E[Y(0)\mid X = c]$ for the RD effect, with both conditional expectation functions continuous at $c$.
(S2) Estimation. p. 3 (PDF p. 3): “The standard way to proceed is to assume that the potential outcome functions are smooth, meaning that they do not change too quickly. This implies that observations close to the cutoff are somewhat informative of the value of the functions at the cutoff, so they can be used for estimation.” and “We can interpret this as a bias–variance trade-off, where the bias is governed by the relevance of the observations and the variance by their numbers.” No smoothness class, bound or rate is stated.
(S3) Inference. p. 3 (PDF p. 3): “To conduct hypothesis tests or construct confidence intervals, researchers need to estimate the accuracy of the RD point estimate. Conventional methods used to gauge this accuracy rely on an assumption that the bias of the estimator is negligible compared to its variance, as would be the case in, for example, a randomized experiment. However, when a bandwidth selection method balances bias and variance to maximize accuracy, the bias is not negligible, and it must therefore be accounted for when drawing inference. Researchers sometimes neglect doing so, with the consequence that their hypothesis tests and confidence intervals are misleading even when the sample is large.” The three remedies the paper recognizes, pp. 3–4 (PDF pp. 3–4): “The first approach is so-called undersmoothing, meaning that one uses a bandwidth that is smaller than the optimal one. If done correctly, this will ensure that the bias indeed is negligible in large samples, so researchers can use conventional methods to construct hypothesis tests and confidence intervals.”; “The second approach is to adjust the inference procedure for the bias. […] The alternative approach described by Calonico et al. (2014), which is becoming the standard approach used in political science, is to also estimate the precision of the bias adjustment and incorporate this into the variance estimator. This allows researchers to use bias adjustments that have similar precision as the point estimator (e.g., as would be the case when the same bandwidth is used for both point and bias estimation), and it should improve finite sample performance.”; “The third approach is to adjust the inference procedure with the worse-case bias consistent with the observed data. The worst-case is taken with respect to a stipulated class of functions, in which the true conditional expectation function is assumed to exist.”
(S4) Sample and $t$-statistics. p. 4 (PDF p. 4): “There were 45 studies in total that satisfied these inclusion criteria.” and “Figure 1 presents the distribution of $t$-statistics for the published findings among all 45 studies in our sample. The first panel presents the distribution of the main reported result of each article, meaning that each article contributes one $t$-statistic. The second panel presents the distribution of all results that were referenced in the articles’ abstracts, which we take as a proxy for being a primary result of an article. There are 80 $t$-statistics in total in the second panel, meaning that each article contributes 1.78 statistics on average. To avoid overrepresentation of articles that present many results, the $t$-statistics in the second panel are weighted by the inverse of the total number of results in each study. For the majority of the studies, we either use reported $t$-statistics or reconstruct $t$-statistics using the ratio of coefficients and standard errors. For the small number of the studies where neither $t$-statistics nor standard errors were reported, we reconstruct $t$-statistics using reported $p$-values, confidence intervals and point estimates, or using replication code and data provided by the authors.” The horizontal axis of the histograms is labelled ‘t−statistic’, with ticks 0.98, 1.96, 2.94, 3.92; that the plotted and tested statistics are absolute values is read from the replication code, not from the text.
(S5) Reanalysis. p. 7 (PDF p. 7), Methodology: “We were able to obtain such data for 36 out of the 45 studies in our sample.”; “Our primary reanalysis uses the default settings in the R package rdrobust (Calonico et al., 2015). The procedure implemented in this package has well-understood theoretical properties and attempts to address the concerns discussed in the \emph{Why is it hard to estimate RD effects?} section. The reanalysis results we present in the main body of the paper exclude all studies that originally used the rdrobust package to estimate the effects, as a reanalysis would bring few new insights for these studies. This results in 39 estimates across 25 studies.”; “One limitation of the approach by Calonico et al. (2015) is that it is motivated by an asymptotic approximation. This means that confidence intervals and hypothesis tests may not be valid in finite samples.” The three panels of Figures 3 and 4 (p. 7, Results) are: the original analyses; “the default bandwidth selection method implemented in rdrobust (“mserd”)” with no “adjustments for bias for the point estimator nor any adjustments for the standard errors”; and the same bandwidth selection with “the bias adjustment for the point estimator” and estimated standard errors adjusted “to account for the added imprecision of the bias adjustment”.
(S6) Power analysis. p. 9 (PDF p. 9): “To investigate the extent to which this is a relevant concern among RD studies in political science, we conducted retrospective power analyses for all 36 studies with replication data, comprising 64 separate analyses. Using the power analysis method implemented in the R package rdpower by Cattaneo et al. (2019), we estimate the power of a two-tailed test at the 5% significance level based on a central limit approximation for the sampling distribution. The power analyses presume that $p$-values will be constructed with the bias adjustment and robust standard errors as implemented by rdrobust. As this procedure is only asymptotically valid, our power calculations may be optimistic relative to approaches that control the false positive rate in finite samples.”; “We measure effect size by Cohen’s $d$, which is the treatment effect standardized by the standard deviation of the outcome (Cohen, 1988). We use the standard deviation of the outcome of control units within the default bandwidth in the rdrobust package for this standardization. We investigate the effect sizes 0.1, 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8.”; “Table 2 presents the results from the power analyses. The cells give the proportion of the 64 analyses that attain the power specified by the columns for the effect size specified by the rows. For example, we see that only 17% of the analyses attain 60% power to detect a standardized effect of 0.1. We weigh the analyses in the same way as in Figure 1(b) to account for the fact that some studies conducted more analyses than others.”
(S7) Notation of the targets that is not in the paper. $\Phi$ and $\varphi$ are the distribution function and density of $N(0,1)$. $z = \Phi^{-1}(39/40)$ is the two-sided 5% normal critical value; the paper prints its rounding $1.96 = 49/25$ and the replication code uses the unrounded quantile ($1.95996398454000 < z < 1.95996398454010$). The normal-approximation power of the two-tailed 5% test of (S6), for a statistic distributed $N(\tau/s, 1)$ with $s > 0$, is $f(|\tau|/s)$ with $$f(a) = \Phi(a - z) + \Phi(-a - z), \qquad a \ge 0 .$$ For integers $0 \le k \le n$ and $p \in [0,1]$, $G_{n,k}(p) = \sum_{j=k}^{n} \binom{n}{j} p^j (1-p)^{n-j}$ is the upper tail of the Binomial$(n,p)$ distribution. Where a target takes a number from the deposited replication files (a stored standard error, a count, a weight), it says so and treats the number as a premise; such premises are not part of the mathematics to be proved.

canonical_claim.location: p. 7 (PDF p. 7), Results, right column, paragraph beginning ‘Panel 3(c)’; Abstract, p. 1 (PDF p. 1); Introduction, p. 2 (PDF p. 2), left column; Concluding remarks, p. 10 (PDF p. 10)
canonical_claim.statement:
Pointwise fixed-score/mean-function witnesses showing that estimator comparisons alone do not determine pointwise coverage. Exact coverage at stipulated affine means does not establish validity over the maintained smoothness class or refute the sound conditional bias warning. The older M1/M2 witness is distinct from the new G/L/R exhibits.
Model M1. Running variable $X \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(-1,1)$; cutoff $0$; sharp treatment $D = \mathbf{1}\{X \ge 0\}$; for every unit $Y_i(0) = 2 + X_i + \varepsilon_i$ and $Y_i(1) = 6 + X_i + \varepsilon_i$, where the $\varepsilon_i$ are independent $N(0,1)$ and independent of the $X_i$, and the variance $1$ is known. The conditional expectation functions $E[Y(0)\mid X = x] = 2 + x$ and $E[Y(1)\mid X = x] = 6 + x$ are affine, hence continuous at the cutoff, so the design satisfies (S1) and (S2), and the RD effect is $\tau = 6 - 2 = 4$. All statements are conditional on a sample of eight units with scores $x = \pm j/5$, $j = 1,2,3,4$, one unit at each score; given the scores the eight outcomes are independent, $Y \sim N(2 - u, 1)$ at a left score and $Y \sim N(6 + u, 1)$ at a right score, where $u = |x|$.
Estimators. On each side order the four units by distance $u = (\tfrac15, \tfrac25, \tfrac35, \tfrac45)$ and give them the triangular kernel weights $K(u) = 1 - u = (\tfrac45, \tfrac35, \tfrac25, \tfrac15)$ (bandwidth $h = 1$). Original estimator $A$: the intercept of the kernel-weighted least-squares fit of $Y$ on $(1, u)$ on the right minus the same intercept on the left (local linear, no bias adjustment); its reported standard error is $s_A = \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(A)}$. Replacement estimator $B$ (bias adjustment with the same bandwidth for point and bias estimation, $b = h = 1$): on each side the curvature is estimated by the coefficient on $u^2$ of the kernel-weighted least-squares fit of $Y$ on $(1, u, u^2)$, the estimated bias of the linear intercept is $m$ times that coefficient with $m = \sum_i a_i u_i^2$ ($a$ as in (i)), and $B$ is the right minus the left bias-corrected intercept; its reported standard error is $s_B = \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(B)}$, which includes the variance of the bias estimate and its covariance with the linear intercept.
(i) [Local linear weights] The kernel-weighted Gram matrix of $(1,u)$ is $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 4/5 \\ 4/5 & 2/5 \end{pmatrix}$, with determinant $\tfrac{4}{25}$, and the intercept of the weighted linear fit is $\sum_i a_i Y_i$ with $$a = (\tfrac65, \tfrac{3}{10}, -\tfrac15, -\tfrac{3}{10}), \qquad \sum_i a_i = 1, \quad \sum_i a_i u_i = 0, \quad \sum_i a_i u_i^2 = -\tfrac{21}{125} = m .$$
(ii) [Bias estimate and corrected weights] The kernel-weighted Gram matrix of $(1,u,u^2)$ is $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 4/5 & 2/5 \\ 4/5 & 2/5 & 146/625 \\ 2/5 & 146/625 & 94/625 \end{pmatrix}$, with determinant $\tfrac{168}{390625} > 0$. The coefficient on $u^2$ of the weighted quadratic fit is $\sum_i c_i Y_i$ with $c = (\tfrac{50}{7}, -\tfrac{125}{14}, -\tfrac{25}{7}, \tfrac{75}{14})$, and $\sum_i c_i = 0$, $\sum_i c_i u_i = 0$, $\sum_i c_i u_i^2 = 1$. The estimated bias is $\sum_i d_i Y_i$ with $d = m\,c = (-\tfrac65, \tfrac32, \tfrac35, -\tfrac{9}{10})$, and the bias-corrected intercept is $\sum_i b_i Y_i$ with $$b = a - d = (\tfrac{12}{5}, -\tfrac65, -\tfrac45, \tfrac35), \qquad \sum_i b_i = 1, \quad \sum_i b_i u_i = 0, \quad \sum_i b_i u_i^2 = 0 ;$$ $b$ is also the intercept row of the weighted quadratic fit.
(iii) [Both estimators are unbiased] $A = \sum_{i \in \mathrm{right}} a_i Y_i - \sum_{i \in \mathrm{left}} a_i Y_i$ and $B = \sum_{i \in \mathrm{right}} b_i Y_i - \sum_{i \in \mathrm{left}} b_i Y_i$, and $E[A] = E[B] = 4 = \tau$.
(iv) [Variances] $\mathrm{Var}(A) = 2\sum_i a_i^2 = \tfrac{83}{25}$ and $\mathrm{Var}(B) = 2\sum_i b_i^2 = \tfrac{82}{5}$, so $s_A = \sqrt{83}/5$, $s_B = \sqrt{410}/5$ and $\mathrm{Var}(B)/\mathrm{Var}(A) = \tfrac{410}{83} > 1$. On one side, $\mathrm{Var}(\sum_i a_i Y_i) = \tfrac{83}{50}$, $\mathrm{Var}(\sum_i d_i Y_i) = \tfrac{243}{50}$, $\mathrm{Cov}(\sum_i a_i Y_i, \sum_i d_i Y_i) = -\tfrac{21}{25}$, and $\tfrac{83}{50} + \tfrac{243}{50} - 2(-\tfrac{21}{25}) = \tfrac{41}{5} = \mathrm{Var}(\sum_i b_i Y_i)$.
(v) [Exact inference for both] $(A - 4)/s_A \sim N(0,1)$ and $(B - 4)/s_B \sim N(0,1)$. Hence, with $z = \Phi^{-1}(39/40)$, each of the intervals $[A - z s_A, A + z s_A]$ and $[B - z s_B, B + z s_B]$ contains $\tau = 4$ with probability exactly $\tfrac{19}{20}$; with the printed critical value $\tfrac{49}{25}$ in place of $z$ both coverage probabilities equal $2\Phi(\tfrac{49}{25}) - 1$.
(vi) [A realization in which the reanalysis loses significance] Take the outcomes $Y = (\tfrac{19}{10}, \tfrac32, \tfrac85, 1)$ at $x = (-\tfrac15, -\tfrac25, -\tfrac35, -\tfrac45)$ and $Y = (\tfrac{63}{10}, \tfrac{63}{10}, \tfrac{34}{5}, \tfrac{33}{5})$ at $x = (\tfrac15, \tfrac25, \tfrac35, \tfrac45)$ (errors $(\tfrac{1}{10}, -\tfrac{1}{10}, \tfrac15, -\tfrac15)$ on each side). The linear intercepts are $\tfrac{211}{100}$ (left) and $\tfrac{611}{100}$ (right); the bias-corrected intercepts are $\tfrac{52}{25}$ and $\tfrac{152}{25}$; so $A = B = 4$. The squared $t$-statistics for the hypothesis of a zero effect are $t_A^2 = 16/\tfrac{83}{25} = \tfrac{400}{83}$ and $t_B^2 = 16/\tfrac{82}{5} = \tfrac{40}{41}$, and $$\tfrac{40}{41} < \left(\tfrac{49}{25}\right)^2 = \tfrac{2401}{625} < \tfrac{400}{83},$$ that is, $|t_B| < 1.96 < |t_A|$.
Conclusion. In M1 the reanalysis has a larger standard error ($s_B > s_A$), a smaller absolute $t$-statistic and no significance at $1.96$ where the original analysis had it, although the original analysis did not overestimate its accuracy in any sense: $A$ is unbiased, $s_A$ is the exact sampling standard deviation of $A$, and the original 95% interval has exact coverage. So a larger replacement standard error and a leftward shift of the $t$-statistic do not imply that the original standard error was too small or that the original inference was miscalibrated.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper. The RD effect and its identification under continuity: standing assumption (S1). The two analyses compared, p. 7 (PDF p. 7): “Panel 3(b) reanalyzes all 39 estimates using the default bandwidth selection method implemented in rdrobust (“mserd”) but does not make any adjustments for bias for the point estimator nor any adjustments for the standard errors.” and “Panel 3(c) reanalyzes the studies using the same bandwidth selection method as in the second panel but also implements the bias adjustment for the point estimator and adjusts the estimated standard errors to account for the added imprecision of the bias adjustment. Here, we see a clear shift to the left, indicating that these studies have systematically overestimated the accuracy of their estimates.” The paper does not define ‘accuracy’; p. 3 uses it for what hypothesis tests and confidence intervals are built from (“researchers need to estimate the accuracy of the RD point estimate”), and p. 4 describes bias adjustments “that have similar precision as the point estimator (e.g., as would be the case when the same bandwidth is used for both point and bias estimation)” (S3).
Not in the paper (the validator's construction and reading): Model M1, the eight scores, the triangular kernel with $h = b = 1$, the estimators $A$ and $B$, the known error variance, and the reading of ‘overestimated the accuracy of their estimates’ as: the reported standard error is smaller than the sampling standard deviation of the estimator, or the nominal 95% interval contains the RD effect with probability below 95%. Fact used in (v): if $\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_k$ are independent $N(0,1)$ and $w \in \mathbb{R}^k$, $w \ne 0$, then $\sum_j w_j \varepsilon_j \sim N(0, \sum_j w_j^2)$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The diagnosis of the Abstract (p. 1), of the Introduction (p. 2), of the Results paragraph on Panel 3(c) (p. 7) and of the Concluding remarks (p. 10, ‘More than half of the studies in our sample do not properly estimate the accuracy of their estimates’), as repaired by Sol: the reanalysis is consistent with understated original uncertainty but does not establish it, nor the fraction of studies affected (formal content: the comparison does not identify the calibration of the original inference)
canonical_claim.location: Abstract, p. 1 (PDF p. 1); p. 2 (PDF p. 2), left column; p. 7 (PDF p. 7), Results, paragraph beginning ‘Panel 3(c)’; Concluding remarks, p. 10 (PDF p. 10)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed; Abstract, p. 1] “However, researchers tend to use inappropriate methods for inference, rendering standard errors artificially small.” [Printed; p. 2] “The reanalysis does not meaningfully change the reported point estimates, but the estimated standard errors become larger on average, moving the $t$-statistics closer to zero. This indicates that the body of published RD studies tends to systematically overestimate the accuracy of their findings.” [Printed; p. 7] “Here, we see a clear shift to the left, indicating that these studies have systematically overestimated the accuracy of their estimates.” [Printed; p. 10] “More than half of the studies in our sample do not properly estimate the accuracy of their estimates, leading to the associated hypothesis tests and confidence intervals being misleading.”
[Corrected; Sol's smallest_repair (validated.json, P033-N006), verbatim] “Replace the abstract diagnosis, p. 7 indicating-clause and p. 10 majority sentence (and the analogous p. 2 clause) by: Our standardized reanalysis of 25 studies yields larger robust standard errors for 27 of 39 estimates and smaller absolute test statistics for 28 of 39 estimates; standardized standard errors are larger and absolute test statistics smaller on average. This pattern is consistent with understated original uncertainty, but changes in estimators, bandwidths, bias estimation and precision also affect the comparison, which alone does not establish inappropriate original inference or the fraction of studies with misleading tests and confidence intervals. Passage-specific wording is in artifact/proof.md §7.”
[Passage-specific wording; doubt/artifact/proof.md, section 7, verbatim] Abstract: “Our standardized reanalysis often produces larger estimated standard errors and smaller absolute test statistics than the original analyses. This pattern is consistent with understated uncertainty in the original findings, but it does not by itself establish inappropriate original inference.” Page 7: “Under the standardized bias-corrected analysis, the distribution shifts to the left. This pattern is consistent with understated original uncertainty, but changes in estimator, bandwidth and the precision of bias estimation also affect it; the comparison alone does not establish that the original analyses were miscalibrated.” Page 10: “In our standardized reanalysis of 25 studies, robust standard errors exceed the original estimates for 27 of 39 estimates, and 28 of the 39 absolute test statistics are smaller. Standardized standard errors are larger on average and absolute test statistics are smaller on average. These changes are consistent with concerns about understated uncertainty, but do not establish the fraction of original studies with misleading tests or confidence intervals.” The counts in these sentences (25 studies, 27 of 39, 28 of 39) are read from the deposited results and are not part of the formal statement.
[Formal content of the corrected claim, with every hypothesis] Notation and Model M1 as in P033-T1: eight units at the scores $x = \pm j/5$, $j = 1,\dots,4$; original estimator $A$ with reported standard error $s_A = \sqrt{83}/5$; replacement estimator $B$ with $s_B = \sqrt{410}/5$.
(a) [The ratio of two correct standard errors carries no information on calibration] If $A \sim N(\tau, \sigma_A^2)$ and $B \sim N(\tau, \sigma_B^2)$ with $\sigma_A, \sigma_B > 0$ (no condition on their joint distribution or on $\sigma_B/\sigma_A$), then for every $c > 0$ $$P(|A - \tau| \le c\,\sigma_A) = P(|B - \tau| \le c\,\sigma_B) = 2\Phi(c) - 1 .$$
(b) [A second model with the same law of the data] Model M2 keeps the score distribution, the control mean $E[Y(0)\mid X = x] = 2 + x$ and the error law of M1 and sets $E[Y(1)\mid X = x] = 6 + x + q(x)$ with $$q(x) = 20\,(1 - 5x)(1 - \tfrac52 x)(1 - \tfrac53 x)(1 - \tfrac54 x) = 20 - \tfrac{625}{3}x + \tfrac{4375}{6}x^2 - \tfrac{3125}{3}x^3 + \tfrac{3125}{6}x^4 .$$ $q$ is a polynomial, so both conditional expectation functions of M2 are continuous and smooth; $q(j/5) = 0$ for $j = 1,2,3,4$ and $q(0) = 20$, so the RD effect of M2 is $\tau_2 = 26 - 2 = 24$. Conditional on the eight scores, the vector of the eight outcomes has the same distribution under M1 and under M2 (independent normal variables with variance $1$ and means $2 - u$ on the left and $6 + u$ on the right). Consequently every statistic computed from the scores, the treatment indicators and the outcomes, in particular $(A, s_A, B, s_B)$, both $t$-statistics and every comparison of them, has the same conditional distribution under M1 and under M2.
(c) [In M2 the original inference fails] Under M2, $E[A] = 4$, so $A$ has bias $-20$ for $\tau_2 = 24$, and $Z_A = (A - 4)/s_A \sim N(0,1)$. For a critical value $\kappa > 0$ the event $\{24 \in [A - \kappa s_A, A + \kappa s_A]\}$ is contained in $\{Z_A \ge 20/s_A - \kappa\}$. For $\kappa = \tfrac{49}{25}$: $(20/s_A)^2 = \tfrac{10000}{83} > \tfrac{30276}{625} = (5 + \tfrac{49}{25})^2$, so $20/s_A - \kappa > 5$ and, by Chebyshev's inequality with $E[Z_A^2] = 1$, $$P_{M2}\big(24 \in [A - \tfrac{49}{25} s_A,\ A + \tfrac{49}{25} s_A]\big) \le P(|Z_A| \ge 5) \le \tfrac{1}{25} .$$ For $\kappa = z = \Phi^{-1}(39/40)$: $z < 5$ (because $\Phi(5) \ge \tfrac{49}{50} > \tfrac{39}{40}$) and $20/s_A > 10$ (because $\tfrac{10000}{83} > 100$), so the coverage probability is again at most $\tfrac{1}{25}$.
(d) [In M1 it is exact] Under M1 the same interval contains $\tau = 4$ with probability $2\Phi(\tfrac{49}{25}) - 1 \ge 1 - (\tfrac{25}{49})^2 = \tfrac{1776}{2401} > \tfrac{1}{25}$, and with probability exactly $\tfrac{19}{20}$ when $z$ is used (P033-T1 (v)).
(e) [Neither the calibration nor the fraction of miscalibrated studies is determined by the comparison] Let $N \ge 1$ studies be independent, each with eight units at the scores above, and let $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$; study $j$ follows M2 if $j \in S$ and M1 otherwise. The joint conditional distribution of all outcomes, and therefore of the $N$ comparisons of original with replacement estimates, standard errors and $t$-statistics, does not depend on $S$, while the number of studies whose original 95% interval covers its own RD effect with probability at most $\tfrac{1}{25}$ is $|S|$ and the number whose original interval has exact coverage $\tfrac{19}{20}$ is $N - |S|$. Hence every statistic computed from the data has the same distribution for all $S$, and no statistic equals $|S|$ with probability one under every $S$; in particular the comparison cannot distinguish $S = \emptyset$ (no study miscalibrated) from $S = \{1,\dots,N\}$ (all miscalibrated), and it cannot establish that the fraction $|S|/N$ exceeds $\tfrac12$.
(f) [Why the bias-corrected standard error is a different quantity] For square-integrable $L$ (a point estimate) and $\hat{\beta}$ (an estimate of its bias), $\mathrm{Var}(L - \hat{\beta}) = \mathrm{Var}(L) + \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\beta}) - 2\,\mathrm{Cov}(L, \hat{\beta})$; in P033-T1, on each side, $\tfrac{41}{5} = \tfrac{83}{50} + \tfrac{243}{50} + \tfrac{42}{25}$. The standard error of the corrected estimator measures the sampling variability of $L - \hat{\beta}$; it is not a statement about the variance of $L$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper: standing assumptions (S1)–(S3) and (S5). The paper names no count as the basis of ‘More than half of the studies in our sample’; the sample is the 45 surveyed studies (p. 4), of which 25 (39 estimates) enter the main reanalysis (p. 7). Qualifications the paper itself attaches: p. 7, “One limitation of the approach by Calonico et al. (2015) is that it is motivated by an asymptotic approximation. This means that confidence intervals and hypothesis tests may not be valid in finite samples.”; pp. 7–8, “The standard errors are systematically larger in Figure 4(b) than in Figure 4(a). This is partly because some studies use global polynomial specifications to estimate the RD effect. A global polynomial specification does not impose any bandwidth restriction on the sample, making the bandwidth selected by rdrobust dramatically smaller, leading to larger standard errors. The standard errors are even larger in Figure 4(c), reflecting the added imprecision introduced by the bias adjustment.”
Not in the paper: Models M1 and M2, the estimators $A$ and $B$ (P033-T1), and the formalization of ‘the comparison alone does not establish’ as non-identification: two data-generating processes that satisfy the paper's RD assumptions, induce the same distribution of everything the reanalysis computes, and differ in whether the original interval is calibrated. Chebyshev's inequality is used in the form $P(|Z| \ge t) \le E[Z^2]/t^2$.
canonical_claim.note: The diagnosis is limited by the empirical-support gap; the paper’s maintained smoothness/continuity standard and conditional warning about neglected bias are sound. Existing fixed-model statements concern pointwise calibration, not uniform validity over that class. The undocumented majority remains unestablished.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The standard errors of the reanalysis for clustered designs (p. 7, ‘Our primary reanalysis uses the default settings in the R package rdrobust’; p. 9, ‘the bias adjustment and robust standard errors as implemented by rdrobust’), read as estimates of the sampling uncertainty of the clustered estimates; the witness is the adjudicating validator's construction and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 7 (PDF p. 7), Methodology; p. 9 (PDF p. 9), Power analysis and Table 2; Table 3, p. 10 (PDF p. 10); Figures 3 and 4, p. 8 (PDF p. 8)
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact counterexample (the adjudicating validator's construction; not in the paper): a clustered sharp RD design with constant conditional means, bounded outcomes and independent clusters in which the default nearest-neighbour cluster-robust variance estimate equals $0$ for every possible outcome vector, while the true sampling variances of the conventional and of the bias-corrected estimator are $\tfrac{62}{25}$ and $10$.
Design. Ten clusters $g = 1, \dots, 10$ with running-variable values $x_g = (-5, -4, -3, -2, -1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)$, in this order; each cluster has five records, all with $x = x_g$ (so every $x$-cell has $m = 5$ records and lies inside one cluster). Cutoff $0$, $D = \mathbf{1}\{x \ge 0\}$; bandwidths $h = b = 6$; triangular kernel $K(x) = 1 - |x|/6$; local linear point estimation ($p = 1$) and local quadratic bias estimation ($q = 2$). Outcomes: $U_1, \dots, U_{10}$ are independent, each uniform on $\{-1, +1\}$, and every record of cluster $g$ has $Y(0) = Y(1) = U_g$, so that $Y_{gi} = U_g$ for $i = 1, \dots, 5$. Both conditional expectation functions are identically $0$, and the RD effect is $0$. The $2^{10} = 1024$ outcome vectors are equally likely.

[Corrected; Sol's smallest_repair (validated.json, P033-N011), verbatim] “Qualify the use of the default residual method for clustered designs with repeated running-variable cells. Replace individual within-cell NN residuals by a variance construction that preserves cluster-level uncertainty, retain specified clusters and joint scores when clusters span the cutoff, propagate the change through bandwidth selection and power estimation, and regenerate affected reanalysis displays and numerical summaries. Regression plug-in residuals such as clustered HC1 illustrate removal of the cancellation while leaving the RD estimand unchanged. Keeping the original algorithm would require an actual restriction preventing this design-induced cancellation; merely assuming many clusters, smooth means, bounded moments or positive-definite covariance does not suffice.”
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis] Definitions of the nearest-neighbour residual $r_i$ and of the cluster-robust variance estimate $\hat V$ as in definitions_needed.
(i) [Cancellation identity] Let $m \ge 2$, let $y_1, \dots, y_m$ be real numbers, $S = \sum_j y_j$, and $r_i = \sqrt{\tfrac{m-1}{m}}\,\big(y_i - \tfrac{S - y_i}{m-1}\big)$. Then $r_i = \sqrt{\tfrac{m}{m-1}}\,\big(y_i - \tfrac{S}{m}\big)$ for every $i$, and $\sum_{i=1}^m r_i = 0$.
(ii) [A nested cell contributes nothing to the cluster score] Suppose every $x$-cell in the estimation window has at least four records, so that $r_i$ is given by the formula of (i) within its cell. Let $\ell$ be any real-valued function of $x$. If a cell $C$ with common value $x_C$ is contained in a cluster $g$, then $\sum_{i \in C} \ell(x_i)\, r_i = \ell(x_C) \sum_{i \in C} r_i = 0$. If every cell that meets $g$ is contained in $g$, then the cluster score $\sum_{i \in g} \ell(x_i)\, r_i$ is $0$. If this holds for every cluster, then $\hat V = f \sum_g \big(\sum_{i \in g} \ell(x_i) r_i\big)^2 = 0$ for every outcome vector and every factor $f$, for the conventional and for the bias-corrected weights alike.
(iii) [Many clusters, a shrinking bandwidth and smooth means do not repair it] For an integer $n \ge 3$ put $n(n+1)$ clusters on each side of the cutoff $0$ at distances $j/[n(n+1)]$, $j = 1, \dots, n(n+1)$, five records per cluster, bandwidths $h = b = 1/n$, triangular kernel, and outcomes as in P033-T3 ($Y_{gi} = U_g$ with independent signs $U_g$). Exactly $n$ clusters per side have positive kernel weight, namely $w_j = 1 - u_j$ with $u_j = j/(n+1)$, $j = 1, \dots, n$. With $S_0 = \sum_j w_j$, $S_1 = \sum_j w_j u_j$, $S_2 = \sum_j w_j u_j^2$: $$S_0 = \frac n2, \quad S_1 = \frac{n(n+2)}{6(n+1)}, \quad S_2 = \frac{n(n+2)}{12(n+1)}, \quad S_0 S_2 - S_1^2 = \frac{n^2(n+2)(n-1)}{72(n+1)^2} > 0,$$ the one-side intercept of the kernel-weighted linear fit is $\sum_{j=1}^n a_j U_j$ with $$a_j = \frac{w_j (S_2 - S_1 u_j)}{S_0 S_2 - S_1^2} = \frac{6\,(n+1-j)(n+1-2j)}{n(n-1)(n+1)},$$ $\sum_{j=1}^n (n+1-j)^2 (n+1-2j)^2 = \tfrac{1}{30}\, n(n-1)(n+1)(4n^2+5n-1)$, and the conventional estimator (right minus left intercept) has true variance $$V_n = 2\sum_{j=1}^n a_j^2 = \frac{12\,(4n^2+5n-1)}{5\,n(n-1)(n+1)} > 0, \qquad n V_n \to \frac{48}{5} \ \ (n \to \infty),$$ while the nearest-neighbour variance estimate equals $0$ for every outcome vector at every $n$. With the independent record noise of P033-T3 (v) the true variance is $\tfrac65 V_n$ and the estimate is still $0$.
(iv) [A variance construction that keeps the cluster component] Let $Z_1, \dots, Z_G$ ($G \ge 2$) be independent with a common mean and a common variance $\sigma_Z^2$, let $\bar Z = G^{-1}\sum_g Z_g$ and let $a \in \mathbb{R}^G$. Then $E[(Z_g - \bar Z)^2] = (1 - \tfrac1G)\,\sigma_Z^2$ and $$E\Big[\frac{G}{G-1}\sum_{g=1}^G a_g^2 (Z_g - \bar Z)^2\Big] = \sigma_Z^2 \sum_{g=1}^G a_g^2 = \mathrm{Var}\Big(\sum_{g=1}^G a_g Z_g\Big).$$ In P033-T3, with $Z_g$ the cluster mean outcome and $G = 10$, this expectation is $\tfrac{62}{25}$ and $10$ for $a$ and $a^{\mathrm{bc}}$, and $\tfrac{372}{125}$ and $12$ with the record noise of P033-T3 (v).

Then the corrected shares are $$\big(\tfrac16 - \tfrac1{36},\ \tfrac{11}{72} - \tfrac1{36},\ \tfrac5{48} - \tfrac1{36}\big) = \big(\tfrac5{36}, \tfrac18, \tfrac{11}{144}\big), \qquad \big(\tfrac1{13} - \tfrac1{26},\ \tfrac1{13} - \tfrac1{26},\ \tfrac1{26} - \tfrac1{26}\big) = \big(\tfrac1{26}, \tfrac1{26}, 0\big),$$ so that Table 2's row $0.17 \mid 0.15 \mid 0.10$ becomes about $0.14 \mid 0.125 \mid 0.08$, the election row $0.08 \mid 0.08 \mid 0.04$ becomes $0.04 \mid 0.04 \mid 0.00$, and ‘only 17%’ becomes about 14% ($\tfrac{5}{36} = 0.1388\ldots$).

canonical_claim.statement:
Exact counterexample (the validator's construction; not in the paper): a fuzzy design with binary individual outcomes, recorded as cell counts, in which the effect divided by the standard deviation of the counts is not Cohen's $d$ of the individual outcome and changes when the cells are made larger, while the individual effect and the individual standard deviation do not change.
Design. On each side of an eligibility cutoff there are two equally likely cell types, each cell containing 100 individuals with binary outcomes. Eligible side: 50 prior-year voters in each cell; the numbers of future voters in the two cells are $10$ and $50$. Ineligible side: no prior-year voters; the numbers of future voters are $10$ and $40$. Individual-level construction: each eligible cell has 50 compliers, exactly 5 of whom are induced to vote in the future by prior voting; without treatment the two eligible cells would have 5 and 45 future voters; every potential outcome is 0 or 1.
(i) [The effect] The cell means are: prior voters $50$ (eligible) and $0$ (ineligible); future voters $\tfrac{10+50}{2} = 30$ (eligible) and $\tfrac{10+40}{2} = 25$ (ineligible). The fuzzy (Wald) effect is $\tfrac{30 - 25}{50 - 0} = \tfrac{1}{10}$, an effect on an individual's probability of voting.
(ii) [Cohen's $d$ of the individual outcome] In the untreated (ineligible) population the outcome has mean $p_0 = \tfrac{10 + 40}{200} = \tfrac14$ and variance $p_0(1 - p_0) = \tfrac{3}{16}$, so $d^2 = (\tfrac{1}{10})^2 / \tfrac{3}{16} = \tfrac{4}{75}$.
(iii) [What the count standardization gives] The sample variance of the two future-voter counts on the eligible side (the side the code treats as control) is $\tfrac{(10-30)^2 + (50-30)^2}{2-1} = 800$, which gives $d_{\mathrm{count}}^2 = (\tfrac{1}{10})^2/800 = \tfrac{1}{80000} \ne \tfrac{4}{75}$. Using the other side does not repair it: there the sample variance of the counts is $\tfrac{(10-25)^2 + (40-25)^2}{2-1} = 450$.
(iv) [Dependence on the size of the cells] Double every cell (200 individuals, all counts doubled). The Wald effect is $\tfrac{60 - 50}{100 - 0} = \tfrac{1}{10}$, $p_0 = \tfrac14$ and $d^2 = \tfrac{4}{75}$ are unchanged, but the sample variance of the eligible-side counts is $\tfrac{(20-60)^2 + (100-60)^2}{2-1} = 3200$ and $d_{\mathrm{count}}^2 = \tfrac{1}{320000}$, one quarter of its former value.
(v) [In general] For any $\lambda > 0$, multiplying every outcome count and every treatment count by $\lambda$ leaves the Wald ratio unchanged, $\tfrac{\lambda(\bar Y_E - \bar Y_I)}{\lambda(\bar D_E - \bar D_I)} = \tfrac{\bar Y_E - \bar Y_I}{\bar D_E - \bar D_I}$, and multiplies the sample standard deviation of the outcome counts by $\lambda$; so the count-standardized effect is multiplied by $1/\lambda$.

For a sample of $N \ge 2$ binary values with mean $\hat p$, the sample variance with divisor $N - 1$ is $\tfrac{N}{N-1}\hat p(1 - \hat p) \le \tfrac{N}{4(N-1)}$. Hence an effect of $d = 0.1$ standard deviations of a binary individual outcome satisfies $|\tau| = 0.1\,\mathrm{SD} \le \tfrac{1}{20}$ in the population, and $|\tau| \le \tfrac{1}{20}\sqrt{N/(N-1)}$ with a sample standard deviation. The effect implied by the count standardization, $2.458$, is not a possible difference of two probabilities, which is at most $1$ in absolute value.
(ii) [The power function is increasing] With $z = \Phi^{-1}(39/40)$ and $f(a) = \Phi(a - z) + \Phi(-a - z)$: $f(0) = \tfrac{1}{20}$, $f'(a) = \varphi(a - z) - \varphi(a + z) > 0$ for $a > 0$, so $f$ is strictly increasing on $[0, \infty)$; and $f(a) < \Phi(a - z) + \tfrac{1}{40}$ for $a > 0$.

For every $|\tau| \le \tfrac{1}{20}$, the normal-approximation power of (S6) satisfies $$f(|\tau|/s) \le f\big(\tfrac{1}{20 s}\big), \qquad 0.8972619 < f\big(\tfrac{1}{20 s}\big) < 0.8972620, \qquad\text{in particular } f(|\tau|/s) < \tfrac{19}{20},$$ where $\tfrac{1}{20s} = 3.2260664\ldots$ and $\tfrac{1}{20s} - z = 1.2661024\ldots$. Equivalently, the standard deviation $\sigma$ for which $f(0.1\,\sigma/s)$ equals $0.60$, $0.80$ and $0.95$ is $0.3430295\ldots$, $0.4342101\ldots$ and $0.5587016\ldots$ respectively, and the last exceeds $\tfrac12$. With the sample bound of (i) and $N \ge 31731$ (the validator's lower bound for the number of individuals in the local control pool) the standard deviation is at most $0.5000079$ and the power at most $0.8972711 < \tfrac{19}{20}$.

canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed; p. 5] “The test compares the number of studies just above and just below the 1.96 threshold that corresponds to statistical significance at the 5% level. Under the assumption (null hypothesis) that the 5% significance level is irrelevant for researchers’ and editors’ publication decisions, the 1.96 threshold should be immaterial, and we would expect approximately the same number of studies just above and just below it. However, the 1.96 threshold becomes relevant for the publication decision if there is p-hacking or publication bias. In this case, we would not be surprised to see more studies just above the threshold. Following Gerber and Malhotra (2008a, 2008b), we include studies within windows around the cutoff with radii (i.e., half-widths or calipers) of 10%, 15%, and 20% of the threshold itself, here corresponding to 0.196, 0.294, and 0.392, respectively. A smaller window is better targeted towards the 1.96 threshold, but has lower power.” “Table 1 presents the results from the caliper tests. For all three window sizes, there are approximately three times as many studies just above the threshold than just below it. We calculate the probability of observing an imbalance at least this extreme under the null hypothesis of no real pathologies in the RD literature by using a binomial distribution with equal success probability, capturing that we would expect a study to be equally likely to be just above and below the threshold under the null. Following Gerber and Malhotra (2008a, 2008b), the test is one-tailed, reflecting the fact that we feel comfortable ruling out, before seeing the data, that researchers or editors actively favor insignificant findings. The $p$-values of the caliper tests range between 3% and 7%, depending on the window size, indicating that it is unlikely that we would observe this large of an imbalance in the $t$-statistics if there were no real pathologies in the RD literature.” [Printed; Table 1, p. 5, “Caliper tests of imbalance of $t$-statistic among RD studies.”; columns Window, % | Below | Above | $p$-value] 10 | 3 | 9 | 0.073. 15 | 4 | 11 | 0.059. 20 | 5 | 14 | 0.032.
[Corrected; Sol's smallest_repair (validated.json, P033-N004), verbatim] “Identify the actual statistical benchmark and qualify its substantive interpretation: 'Conditional on the number of studies in each caliper, we calculate one-sided binomial tail probabilities under a working null of equal probability mass above and below the threshold. Interpreting these probabilities as evidence of publication bias requires an additional justification that the unselected distribution has approximately equal mass on the two sides, or a sensitivity analysis allowing unequal mass. Publication independence alone does not imply the working null.' Retain Table 1's counts and numbers.” [The second validator's wording of the same repair, verbatim] “Retain the counts and numbers but qualify both caliper paragraphs: 'We use an equal-probability benchmark within each caliper window. Under this benchmark, the one-sided binomial tail probabilities range from 3% to 7%. Interpreting them as calibrated tests of reporting or publication selection additionally requires approximately equal unselected probability mass on the two sides of each window; absence of selection alone does not imply that condition.' Apply the same qualification to the supplementary caliper tests and their null interpretations.”
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis] Setting and notation as in definitions_needed: $X_1, \dots, X_M$ independent with density $f$, all published; $0 < h < c$; $A_h + B_h > 0$.
(i) [The exact conditional law] For every $n$ with $P(N = n) > 0$, conditionally on $N = n$ the count $K$ of statistics above the threshold has the Binomial$(n, p_h)$ distribution; in particular $P(K \ge k \mid N = n) = G_{n,k}(p_h)$.
(ii) [When the benchmark is exact] $p_h = \tfrac12$ if and only if $A_h = B_h$. A sufficient condition is local symmetry, $f(c + u) = f(c - u)$ for $0 < u < h$; in particular a density that is constant on $W_h$.
(iii) [When the one-sided test is conservative] $G_{n,k}(p)$ is nondecreasing in $p$ for all $0 \le k \le n$. If $f$ is nonincreasing on $W_h$, then $A_h \le B_h$, $p_h \le \tfrac12$ and $G_{n,k}(p_h) \le G_{n,k}(\tfrac12)$: the paper's tail probability is then an upper bound on the true one. If $f$ is nondecreasing on $W_h$, the inequalities are reversed.
(iv) [A quantitative bound at a fixed width] If $f(x) \ge a > 0$ for $x \in W_h$ and $|f(x) - f(y)| \le L|x - y|$ for $x, y \in W_h$, then $|A_h - B_h| \le L h^2$, $A_h + B_h \ge 2ha$ and $$\Big|p_h - \frac12\Big| = \frac{|A_h - B_h|}{2(A_h + B_h)} \le \frac{L h}{4a} .$$
(v) [The sense in which ‘approximately the same number’ holds] If $f$ is continuous at $c$ and $f(c) > 0$, then $p_h \to \tfrac12$ as $h \downarrow 0$. If moreover $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then $p_h - \tfrac12 = \dfrac{h f'(c)}{4 f(c)} + o(h)$. Neither statement bounds $|p_h - \tfrac12|$ at $h = 0.196$, $0.294$ or $0.392$ (P033-T7 (iv)).
(vi) [The printed numbers are the benchmark's tails] $G_{12,9}(\tfrac12) = \tfrac{299}{4096}$, $G_{15,11}(\tfrac12) = \tfrac{1941}{32768}$ and $G_{19,14}(\tfrac12) = \tfrac{2083}{65536}$, which round to the printed 0.073, 0.059 and 0.032.

(i) [The power the text describes] If the test statistic is distributed $N(\tau/s, 1)$, with $s > 0$ the fitted bias-corrected robust standard error and $\tau$ the hypothesized effect, then the two-tailed test that rejects when the absolute statistic exceeds $z$ has rejection probability $$P\big(|N(\tau/s, 1)| > z\big) = \Phi(|\tau|/s - z) + \Phi(-|\tau|/s - z) = f(|\tau|/s),$$ and $f(0) = \tfrac{1}{20}$. With Cohen's $d$ and the control standard deviation $\sigma_0$ of (S6), $\tau = d\,\sigma_0$.
(ii) [Strict monotonicity] $f'(a) = \varphi(a - z) - \varphi(a + z) > 0$ for $a > 0$, because $(a + z)^2 - (a - z)^2 = 4az > 0$. Hence $f$ is strictly increasing on $[0, \infty)$, and a value $f(a) \in (\tfrac{1}{20}, 1)$ determines $a$.

canonical_claim.statement:
Exact witnesses (the validator's; not in the paper) against the printed slope of the significance line and against the printed name of the standardizing quantity. Coordinates as in definitions_needed: horizontal $x = |\hat\beta|/s_0$, vertical $y = \mathrm{SE}/s_0$, with $s_0 > 0$.
(i) [The printed slope misclassifies] Take $x = y = \tfrac12$, a point inside the plotted ranges $0 \le x \le 2$, $0 \le y \le 0.8$. Its $t$-statistic is $|t| = x/y = 1 < \tfrac{49}{25}$, so it is not significant at the 5% level. The line through the origin with slope $\tfrac{49}{25}$, $y = \tfrac{49}{25}x$, reaches the height $y = \tfrac12$ at $x = \tfrac{25}{98}$, and $\tfrac12 > \tfrac{25}{98}$: the point lies to the right of that line. So the printed description (slope 1.96, estimates to the right of the line significant) classifies this nonsignificant estimate as significant. On the line with the reciprocal slope, $y = \tfrac{25}{49}x$, the height at $x = \tfrac12$ is $\tfrac{25}{98} < \tfrac12$, and the point lies above that line, on its nonsignificant side.
(ii) [Variance and standard deviation are different divisors] The control outcomes $(0, 2, 4)$ have mean $2$, sample variance $\tfrac{(0-2)^2 + (2-2)^2 + (4-2)^2}{3-1} = 4$ and sample standard deviation $2$. (ii) [It is exactly honest] For every $\theta$ and every $|b| \le 1$, $P_{\theta, b}\big(\theta \in [T - H, T + H]\big) = \Phi(H - b) - \Phi(-H - b) \ge \tfrac{19}{20}$, with equality if and only if $|b| = 1$.
(iii) [The transform] $p_*(T) = 2\Phi(-z|T|/H)$ with $z = \Phi^{-1}(39/40)$, $1.95996398454000 < z < 1.95996398454010$: the paper's conversion applied to the estimate $T$ and the half-length $H$.
(iv) [It over-rejects at level one fifth] Let $q = \Phi^{-1}(9/10)$ ($1.28155156554460 < q < 1.28155156554470$) and $C = Hq/z$ ($1.73022157382648 < C < 1.73022157382677$). [Corrected; Sol's smallest_repair (validated.json, P033-N003), verbatim] “Align the account with the reproduced code: remove 'reported p-values' from the main-text list of t-statistic reconstruction sources; describe interval SEs in S4 as the full interval width divided by twice Phi^{-1}(0.95) for 90% intervals and twice Phi^{-1}(0.975) for 95% intervals; clarify that reported p-values are recorded separately and missing p-values derived by normal approximation. Update the Klasnja-Titiunik raw metadata note to describe width. Leave the released calculations unchanged.”
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis] $\beta$ real, $L < U$, $q > 0$; $s_U = (U - \beta)/q$ and $s_W = (U - L)/(2q)$.
(i) [The corrected rule] For a reported interval $[L, U]$ of nominal level $1 - \alpha$, the imputed standard error is $s_W = \dfrac{U - L}{2\,q_\alpha}$ with $q_\alpha = \Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha/2)$, that is $q = \Phi^{-1}(0.95)$ for a 90% interval and $q = \Phi^{-1}(0.975)$ for a 95% interval; the reconstructed statistic is $|t| = |\beta|/s_W$, and a missing $p$-value is $2\Phi(-|t|)$. The point estimate does not enter $s_W$.
(ii) [When the two rules agree] $2q\,(s_W - s_U) = 2\beta - (L + U)$. Hence $s_W = s_U$ if and only if $\beta = \tfrac{L + U}{2}$, $s_W > s_U$ if and only if $\beta > \tfrac{L+U}{2}$, and $s_W < s_U$ if and only if $\beta < \tfrac{L+U}{2}$.
(iii) [Both recover the standard error of an exact normal interval] If $L = \beta - q s$ and $U = \beta + q s$ for some $s > 0$, then $s_W = s_U = s$.
(iv) [The recorded Klašnja and Titiunik row under the corrected rule] With $\beta = -\tfrac{3}{20}$, $L = -\tfrac{213}{1000}$, $U = -\tfrac{101}{1000}$: $s_W = \tfrac{7}{125\,q}$ and $|t_W| = \tfrac{75\,q}{28}$; at $q = \tfrac{49}{25}$ these are $\tfrac{1}{35}$ and $\tfrac{21}{4}$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The diagnosis of original inference, as printed: Abstract (‘rendering standard errors artificially small’), Introduction (p. 2), Results on Panel 3(c) (p. 7) and Concluding remarks (‘More than half of the studies in our sample’, p. 10)
canonical_claim.location: Abstract, p. 1 (PDF p. 1); p. 2 (PDF p. 2), left column; p. 7 (PDF p. 7), Results; p. 10 (PDF p. 10), Concluding remarks
canonical_claim.statement:
[Abstract, p. 1] “A reanalysis of all studies with available data suggests that researcher discretion is not a major driver of these features. However, researchers tend to use inappropriate methods for inference, rendering standard errors artificially small.”
[Introduction, p. 2] “We next reanalyze all studies with available data in order to investigate the consequences of using inappropriate statistical procedures on the distribution of published results. Our reanalysis uses a standardized procedure based on current state of the art methods (Calonico et al., 2015). This aims to correct potential methodological shortcomings in studies using older methods and procedures, and to remove discretion in the analysis. The reanalysis does not meaningfully change the reported point estimates, but the estimated standard errors become larger on average, moving the $t$-statistics closer to zero. This indicates that the body of published RD studies tends to systematically overestimate the accuracy of their findings.”
[Results, p. 7] “Panel 3(b) reanalyzes all 39 estimates using the default bandwidth selection method implemented in rdrobust (“mserd”) but does not make any adjustments for bias for the point estimator nor any adjustments for the standard errors. For this reason, these t-statistics will be too large as the accuracy of estimates is overestimated, potentially making them misleading.” and “Panel 3(c) reanalyzes the studies using the same bandwidth selection method as in the second panel but also implements the bias adjustment for the point estimator and adjusts the estimated standard errors to account for the added imprecision of the bias adjustment. Here, we see a clear shift to the left, indicating that these studies have systematically overestimated the accuracy of their estimates.”
[Concluding remarks, p. 10] “More than half of the studies in our sample do not properly estimate the accuracy of their estimates, leading to the associated hypothesis tests and confidence intervals being misleading.”
[Qualifications the paper attaches; pp. 7–8] “We find that the reanalysis does not systematically change point estimates, but it does have meaningful consequences for the estimated standard errors. The standard errors are systematically larger in Figure 4(b) than in Figure 4(a). This is partly because some studies use global polynomial specifications to estimate the RD effect. A global polynomial specification does not impose any bandwidth restriction on the sample, making the bandwidth selected by rdrobust dramatically smaller, leading to larger standard errors. The standard errors are even larger in Figure 4(c), reflecting the added imprecision introduced by the bias adjustment.”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Standing assumptions (S1)–(S3) and (S5). ‘Accuracy’ is not defined in the paper; ‘our sample’ is the 45 surveyed studies (p. 4), and the reanalysis shown in Figures 3 and 4 covers 39 estimates from 25 of them (p. 7).
canonical_claim.note: An empirical diagnosis and conditional bias warning, not a theorem that any increase in a replacement standard error proves original undercoverage. Pointwise affine examples do not establish model-class validity or identify which original procedures were inappropriate.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The clustered reanalysis with the default settings of rdrobust and the power entries that rest on it, as printed: Methodology (p. 7), Power analysis and Table 2 (p. 9), Table 3, first panel (p. 10)

canonical_claim.statement:
[p. 7] “Our primary reanalysis uses the default settings in the R package rdrobust (Calonico et al., 2015). The procedure implemented in this package has well-understood theoretical properties and attempts to address the concerns discussed in the \emph{Why is it hard to estimate RD effects?} section.”
[p. 9] “Using the power analysis method implemented in the R package rdpower by Cattaneo et al. (2019), we estimate the power of a two-tailed test at the 5% significance level based on a central limit approximation for the sampling distribution. The power analyses presume that $p$-values will be constructed with the bias adjustment and robust standard errors as implemented by rdrobust. As this procedure is only asymptotically valid, our power calculations may be optimistic relative to approaches that control the false positive rate in finite samples.”
[Table 2, p. 9] “Table 2. Proportion of analyses achieving 60%, 80%, and 95% power by effect size.” Column heading “Power (%)” over 60 | 80 | 95; stub heading “% Effect size”. With the sentence “For example, we see that only 17% of the analyses attain 60% power to detect a standardized effect of 0.1.”

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The Cohen's d standardization of the power analysis and the two cells it affects, as printed: p. 9 (definition; Table 2, row 0.1, column 95) and Table 3, second panel (row 0.1, column 95)
canonical_claim.location: p. 9 (PDF p. 9), Power analysis, left column, and Table 2; Table 3, p. 10 (PDF p. 10)
canonical_claim.statement:
[p. 9] “We investigate power with respect to four different effect sizes, ranging from small to large effects. We measure effect size by Cohen’s $d$, which is the treatment effect standardized by the standard deviation of the outcome (Cohen, 1988). We use the standard deviation of the outcome of control units within the default bandwidth in the rdrobust package for this standardization. We investigate the effect sizes 0.1, 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8.”
[Table 2, p. 9, row 0.1, columns 60 | 80 | 95] 0.17 | 0.15 | 0.10. [Table 3, p. 10, ‘Studies not using election data’, row 0.1, columns 60 | 80 | 95] 0.40 | 0.35 | 0.28. The full tables are transcribed in P033-T17.
[The funnel plot that uses a standardization of the same kind; p. 7] “We can disaggregate the information in Figure 3 using a funnel plot, which is a scatter plot with standardized point estimates and standardized estimated standard errors on the two axes. Figure 4 presents such a funnel plot for the 39 estimates in the replication study.$^{3}$ We use the sample variance of the outcome among control units for the standardization.”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Standing assumption (S6). How the standardization was computed for Coppock and Green (2016) is not in the paper; the validator's reading of the deposited files is in the definitions of P033-T5.
canonical_claim.note: The code-defined aggregate fuzzy-IV target is meaningful, while the claimed comparison to individual Cohen’s d uses a different standardization. Preserve the missing individual-SD limitation and all separately established table corrections.
